With 1% defective in this 10,000-item example, how many are defective?
column2:
A flag is not a verdict. — Begin with the whole batch

Our hypothetical batch contains 10,000 items. At a 1% defect rate, 100 are defective and 9,900 are sound. Those groups are the starting denominators for the detector's rates.

100

One percent of 10,000 is 100. The other 9,900 are sound.

A rare condition starts with a small group.

In the stated 1%, 90%, 5% example, which produces more flags?
column2:
A flag is not a verdict. — Apply each rate to its own group

A 90% hit rate flags 90 of the 100 defective items. A 5% false-flag rate flags 495 of the 9,900 sound items. The smaller percentage acts on the much bigger population.

Sound items: 495

Five percent of 9,900 is 495. Ninety percent of 100 is only 90.

Compare counts after multiplying, not percentages alone.

Which denominator belongs to 'defective among flagged items'?
column2:
A flag is not a verdict. — Now stand inside the flagged group

There are 585 flags: 90 true and 495 false. Among those flags, the defective fraction is 90 / 585, about 15.4%.

The detector's 90% hit rate answers a different question: how often it flags an item already known to be defective.

All 585 flagged items

Conditioning on a flag restricts the group to all flagged items, including false flags.

P(defective | flagged) is not P(flagged | defective).

A flag is not a verdict. — Change the base rate, then the false flags

Why can a strong hit rate coexist with a low defective share among flags?
column2:
A flag is not a verdict. — Change the base rate, then the false flags

With the illustrated positive false-flag rate, keep detector rates fixed and raise the defect rate: the flagged group contains a larger defective share. If the false-flag rate is already zero, that share is already 100% and cannot increase. Now set false flags to zero. Every flagged item is defective in this model, but some defective items can still be missed when the hit rate is below 100%.

Defects can be rare. A small false-flag rate on a large sound population can produce more flags than a large hit rate on a small defective population.
  • Apply rates to their own groups
  • Include false flags in the denominator
  • Keep the two conditional directions separate

Base rates and both detector rates matter.
